utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. On behalf of the entire Chamber, I should like to wish all of you good, healthy and hopefully peaceful New Year 2003. Let us hope that the rule of law will be respected by everybody. May the imperative of the rule of law help us, also here in this small courtroom, to overcome all impediments, obstacles, frustrations and even prevent us from making mistakes when bringing this case we hear it today, the 94th day, since April 2002, to a safe and fair end in due time as envisaged, if not even earlier. But please, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we hear the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning, and may I return your good wishes Happy New Year to all Your Honours on behalf of the OTP. It's Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, and Ruth Karper, case manager, this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence wishes you Happy New Year and Merry Christmas. And Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I start with some issues before I give the floor to the parties. And please, tell us immediately that if one or the other party believes that we have to discuss an issue which should be better discussed and more fruitfully discussed in the framework of a 65 ter meeting or in closed session, then please give me a hint. Let us first know, the Defence gave us at the end of last year a list of nine witnesses. We had one additional witness added orally. This would be Witness number 9. I don't want to mention the name because I don't know whether the name is protected or not. It was number 43, 65 ter number 71. Whom can we expect this week and whom next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately, that's true that we are changing the order of our witnesses. And in December, it was mostly due to illnesses of the witnesses. And now, again, we have to change it but mostly because of the Orthodox Christmas and Orthodox New Year. So we have problems for the second week. And we have already informed the Prosecution before this hearing. So we'll submit one motion today, or if you want, I can tell you orally who would be, if you permit our witnesses for the next week. Because it's completely changed, the whole group has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe you can do it immediately after the first break, that we know about the witnesses of next week. But please, can you tell us about witnesses of this week. Is there any change? I heard that we would start with Witness 54, followed by 46, and then 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No changes this week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be limited to the three witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, then, let us hear after the first break what about the next witnesses, because in case there are no other witnesses, we would have to take the initiative and try to call own witnesses in the meantime because there's no day to lose. The parties should be aware that there is no leeway at all. We have to stay in the framework of the time limit as I told you last year in order that this Trial Chamber is ready to start a new case. And so let us wait until the break how to proceed. I have to inform you that the 21st, maybe also the 22nd, there will be a kind of relief for the Defence because Ms. Nada Balaban will appear the 21st. We took care that if need may be, she is also available the 22nd. As you have seen by our decisions, she will appear as a Trial Chamber witness. We have some - I don't want to call it problems - but issues related to new and additional cross-examination. Is it correct that I can declare the problems and the dispute between the parties moot related to Witness Murselovic, whether or not there was a second or even third letter, or whether there was an oral discussion related to this witness. I don't think we need any longer to go into this discussion. We have heard this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the only thing I ought to say because I wasn't here and I had messages relayed to me where I was, I certainly recall a discussion with Mr. Ostojic. I certainly wouldn't have remembered the details because it was in a social connection, when I say social, I mean simply not profession. And I would have expected a letter. That's all I wanted to say. But I'm perfectly willing to accept that he mentioned the name of Murselovic to me, because I gather there was a discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But please, both parties should know that it's not sufficient that the parties discuss these issues. The Chamber should know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, certainly. If it's a formal request, I agree and it should go into writing on both sides. Your Honour, may I just mention while I'm on my feet two connected witnesses who were returning to the Court for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be my next point. We have two witnesses. You indicated this in January in Brdjanin/Talic. At the moment it's only Mr. Brdjanin. And these witnesses would appear on -- we didn't hear anything until now by the Defence whether or not they want to restart the cross-examination of these two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether -- I'm not sure if the first witness was protected and I don't know what his number was. The first witness who is returning is Mr. Sivac. He's coming to testify on Monday in the Brdjanin case. So if the Defence wish to put further questions, which they notify the Trial Chamber and us based on information that was provided to them in the material from the summonses, then perhaps they would be kind enough to let us know because that may be an interruption on the Defence witness schedule if Mr. Sivac is to come back into this Court to be further questioned. But I think Your Honours' ruling was that the questions must be notified in advance and must arise from material that they weren't aware of before in the summonses. Your Honour, the second witness is Mr. Mayhew. I don't know whether the Defence wanted to ask him further questions. He will be testifying in the Brdjanin case next Friday, potentially, although there's a very long witness coming on Tuesday. So it would probably be either the Friday or the Monday. There were -- after he had finished testifying, he was able to point us in the direction of some further documents which we hadn't seen before because they didn't contain his name. These were disclosed to the Defence, so if they want to question him on any of those documents, then he would be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And I think there was also another name you mentioned in an earlier letter that would appear -- person would testify in Brdjanin also in January, not only the person you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- yes. He has not been -- although he was originally schedule -- for some reason I must say I got myself confused bout which witnesses were coming in which case. But the other witness is not actually coming on the 17th of January. I'm not sure when he was coming now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. So please let us know immediately when he will come, and I expect the submission, it may be an oral submission, by the Defence that we immediately know whether or not we have to hear -- the name was already mentioned -- Mr. Sivac. I hope he is not protected. Please let us know that we could correct that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I asked that. I was worried about, that but he isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Whether or not you want to hear Mr. Sivac, do you know already or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. We do, as our correspondence suggested when we wrote on December 4th to the OTP copying the Court, that we would be interested in asking questions of Mr. Sivac deriving strictly from the six testimonies that were provided to us pursuant to Rule 68. We are in the process of preparing written questions at the Court's request and we hope to submit that to the Court by Friday afternoon. We mentioned at the close of last year's session that we prefer not to distribute those questions to the OTP. One, because we consider that to be a work product and we consider it to be privileged. Secondly, we wouldn't want, with all due respect to the OTP, for their witnesses to get an advance notification of the questions we would be asking the witness. But if the Court deems it necessary to provide that to the OTP, then we will have to accept that decision. But we hope to submit the questions and the areas of questioning for Mr. Sivac, again, by this Friday afternoon. It's my understanding he is coming on the 10th to testify in the Brdjanin case. So can we expect him to testify on the 11th in our case, or is it he first testifying here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. He's testifying on Monday which by my reckoning is the 13th. We're not sitting in that case until that week. And he will testify in the Brdjanin case first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the morning, and then it could be possible to hearing in the afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I notice and I am grateful that we seem at the moment to have alternated the two cases, so they are not both sitting at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We tried to do our best with all the assistance of the Registry and that we manage to have this possibility. So I think in principle, the parties should be prepared to hear this witness the 13th of January in the afternoon, provided we get sufficient information related to the questions. What about the questions? May I hear a submission by the OTP whether or not they can live with this procedure of giving the questions first?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is this: That the allegation was that prejudice had been caused because had they had these documents before, they could have asked questions arising from them. What we're concerned about is that this shouldn't be an opportunity to reopen cross-examination based on matters that simply do not arise from the summonses well in the possession of the Defence before. And it may become a matter of argument. Your Honour, we're not anxious to put witnesses through the problem of giving evidence yet again if it's unnecessary. So Your Honour, if it's a matter of law, well then, we would be entitled to see the questions. We would give our undertaking, which I hope would be accepted, that we would not be talking to the witnesses about the questions that they were going to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is self-understanding. And on the other hand, the Defence counsel should know that there is a right to be heard from the side of the OTP. And before we admit the additional cross-examination, also the OTP may give their submission whether or not it's sufficient from their point of view to reopen this cross-examination. Therefore, under this principle rule of the right to be heard, I can't see any possibility to refrain from giving the questions also to the OTP. So we expect your questions, but in principle, the OTP is prepared to present once again Mr. Sivac on Monday afternoon. I think far more important is that what happened in the meantime related to a member of the joint criminal enterprise as we can read it from the fourth amended indictment. And here, the problem emanating from this should be discussed in open court in order that we can take the necessary measures. We can read in paragraph 27 of the fourth amended indictment that it is alleged that Dr. Milomir Stakic, together with Madam Biljana Plavsic, committed crimes in the framework of a criminal enterprise. Until now, all the persons mentioned there had the right to remain silent. In case that there will be a final and binding decision against Madam Biljana Plavsic, we can't no longer apply Rule 90(E) or the principle rule of the right not to testify against herself. So the question is two-fold: First, will one of the party call this then witness in this case? And as we are hearing now the Defence case, the first right would, no doubt, be for the Defence to hear this witness; and in case Defence does not want to hear this witness, we have to decide whether or not it is recommendable, if not mandatory under the jurisprudence related to Rule 98, to hear the alleged partner in the joint criminal enterprise, Madam Biljana Plavsic as soon as possible. This means immediately after the sentencing and before she is leaving The Hague here in this case as a witness. And I don't think there's any right of Ms. Plavsic then to remain silent, and she then can no doubt be compelled to answer the questions. And I think it would be a big mistake not to take this opportunity, if not even duty. Second point emanating from this guilty plea in the end of December is the question to the Prosecution. Of course, the Prosecution appears in front of us as one entity. And if there should be any material which tend to be exculpatory under Rule 68, I would ask the OTP to disclose this material as soon as possible to the Defence and to the Chamber. A third additional point is that admittedly, this Chamber indicated that the Chamber would no longer be prepared to ex officio start another attempt to bring the parties together in order to come to a consensual solution of this case. Maybe in the light of that what happened in the end of December in the case against Biljana Plavsic, this approach may have changed. The Prosecution dropped their allegation of genocide, and there was a request for -- yes, I don't want to comment this, the framework, but for a certain sentence. The question arising from this is whether the Defence, and especially Dr. Stakic, when hearing all this, would be prepared to change their view related to a possible consensual solution, and whether the OTP in the light of this new development would be prepared to rethink their view related to this issue. As time is of essence, and we don't know when there will be this sentencing hearing, and the decision on the sentence, we have to act immediately. And therefore, I want to invite the parties to comment directly on this issue. If you want, we can go into a closed session, but if necessary, I can't see any such desire. So therefore, may I first ask the Prosecution, from their point of view, you know better than all of us, both the content of the arrangement and the possible statements of Ms. Plavsic in the other case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I, as it were, work backwards from the points that Your Honour has just raised. Firstly the question of an agreement with the parties. I ought to make it absolutely clear that the only reason that the allegation of genocide was not pursued against Mrs. Plavsic was because she agreed to plead guilty to persecutions. It is not to say that the Prosecution does not maintain its stance that genocide happened as a result of the criminal enterprise, and indeed it is being pursued against Krajisnik. But the view was taken that as she had volunteered a plea, and I rather think in the light of her age, not to put her on trial in respect of genocide. Your Honour, that's the first point. As far as an agreement between the parties on which this case could be brought to a speedy end, the discussions, as Your Honour knows, have really revolved around the question of the type of sentence that the Prosecution would be seeking, and the type of sentence that the Defence would be seeking as opposed to any difficulty over what the plea would be to. So I really think that's a matter for the Defence to deal with. We made our position clear on the sort of sentence we would be seeking in the event of a plea, and the plea by Mrs. Plavsic doesn't change that at all. Your Honour, in respect of Rule 68 material arising, the sentence hearing itself, of course, was entirely public, I think. And so if anything was said in that, either by Mrs. Plavsic herself or any of the witnesses who came, then that's available to the Defence. She was interviewed before. The Defence have already asked us to look at that interview, and we have been doing so. The difficulty has been that most of apparently what appears in that interview was to the effect that there was no criminal enterprise, and that of course is negated now by her plea of guilty. But we're going to have another check. I've asked, and we rather think there is no Rule 68, but we will check that. As to calling her, at the moment, Your Honour, the Prosecution doesn't have the right to reopen its case in any event. So I think that's really a question for the Defence first of all, and then Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Well, the question to the OTP is whether or not -- I'm not quite sure whether I really got the entire agreement. I only heard and read from this sentencing hearing that she would not be prepared to give any testimony in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But this is not her decision, I think, and it's not subject to any agreement between the OTP and Mrs. Plavsic to decide on this. And can we agree that also the Prosecution is of the opinion that in case she is called by the Defence or by the Chamber, she has to answer and she may be compelled to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After sentencing, Your Honour, that's right. The only reason that was mentioned was whether there would be a reduction or the Prosecution would be willing to give her credit on the basis she would agree to testify. But whether she -- there is no agreement and there could not be that she won't testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Thank you for this. May I hear the Defence on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we, the Defence, believe that Dr. Biljana Plavsic is an important witness. The Court asked a two-fold question. The Defence does not have a right, and it's my understanding from speaking with counsel that she would not appear voluntarily for the Defence. We would ask that the Court do call Biljana Plavsic to testify. I disagree with my learned friend at the OTP that the allegations of joint criminal enterprise are confined to only the count relating to persecutions. If the Court has read the fourth amended indictment, clearly paragraph number 27 is reincorporated within counts 1 and 2 which include both genocide and complicity in genocide. That same joint criminal enterprise, if denied by Dr. Plavsic, may be attributed to those counts as well as the counts of persecution. Therefore, based just upon what the OTP has suggested, they do clearly fall within Rule 68, and we submit that they should be produced. Biljana Plavsic did not give a one hour or a one day interview to the OTP. It's our understanding, based upon information and belief, that it exceeded 15 days of intense interrogation of time periods that do go beyond the parameters of the indictment charged against Dr. Milomir Stakic. We requested before, and we will request again, that the entire interview of Dr. Plavsic be submitted and produced to the Defence and to the Court. With respect to the fact that the OTP maintains their genocide, that interview also becomes important as well as on the count of complicity in genocide. The other counts that remain that we know of are the forcible transfer, and the deportation. Those counts were likewise dropped against Biljana Plavsic, likewise her interviews in connection with those issues would perhaps enlighten us as to why they were dropped and what the position of any coconspirator, as alleged, what their mind set was at the time and what the specific acts of those people were. We would like the Court to call Biljana Plavsic as a witness, and we believe that the Court should do that at a time immediately after her sentencing, but prior to her testimony we would like to get the entirety of her interview with the OTP. I don't think that it's privileged any longer, which a position that they took early on. It's something that a necessity in our opinion because it will promote justice, and it will promote the truth. And the Court in this case specifically since we've alleged and have maintained the position that since Biljana Plavsic and others mentioned in paragraph 27 of the fourth amended complaint are alleged as coconspirators, that information was relevant at the start of this trial, during the OTP's case, and even today after her plea agreement. So we're grateful for the Court to bring this issue up, and we would ask orally and move that that -- the OTP produce her interview to us and that the Court schedule when Biljana Plavsic can testify in this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the joint criminal enterprise relates to genocide as well, but the point is that for Biljana Plavsic to say in her interviews there is no joint criminal enterprise is utterly negated whether it applies to persecutions or genocide by the plea agreement by what she herself said. That's why it's not Rule 68. And it doesn't matter whether it applies to genocide or persecutions. Your Honour, the difficulty is we don't know when sentence is going to take place. And if Your Honour decides to call her as a court witness, then of course we will disclose all the interviews. At the moment our only obligation is to disclose such material as amounts to Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there is more agreement than disagreement between the parties. In case, and we should decide as soon as possible on the issue whether or not to call Ms. Plavsic under Rule 98, then it's not disputed that the Defence and the Trial Chamber has a right to see earlier statements and that all of us can prepare for this testimony. I think it's absolutely necessary immediately to decide on the question whether or not to call this witness, because the necessary preparations have to be done, that she can be heard immediately after the sentencing before she is brought to a third country to serve a possible sentence. So therefore, we will decide without any delay on this, I believe very, very important issue. But I missed any submission by the Defence related to the question of another own initiative on a possible agreement. The Prosecution already made the point that until now, there seems to be no possibility at all from the side of the Defence. But I think from now on, we should discuss the question whether or not to come to such an agreement in open Court. And we should also include Dr. Stakic in person in this -- in the discussion of this question. Maybe, under the impression of the guilty plea of Ms. Plavsic, he also may have changed his point of view related to this. And we would like to hear whether or not we can expect any kind of change in the near future. We can't expect an immediate answer here and today, but there should be a clear answer from the side of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say that if there is going to be perhaps any further discussions, it ought to be in closed session as opposed to in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us please go in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other issues to be discussed before we start with the witness? Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just return to this question of the change of order of the witnesses. I fully understand, and sympathise with the difficulties the Defence have. Can I just make this point? Unlike the Prosecution witnesses where the Defence had all of their statements and indeed previous testimonies if relevant, we have nothing. A constant change like this, as we have had over the last few days, causes two problems, one a major one and one a more minor one. The first is we conduct searches on the basis of what we're told are the up and coming witnesses. The unit that does these searches is obviously inundated with requests, and the only way we can get them done is by saying these witnesses are coming. When there's a sudden complete change, and as I understand there's going to be again next week, that makes it almost impossible for us to do the required research in advance. The summaries we're given are pretty limited in the information that they provide to us and to the Court. And it's obviously right in the interests of justice that the Prosecution should be able to do its searches before the witness is called. So that's the first problem. Your Honour, so I'm going to ask, I understand the difficulties now over the Christmas and New Year Orthodox period, but I would ask in future these changes are kept to an absolute minimum and are not a wholesale as has been happening over the last two weeks. The second matter is this: It causes a problem particularly at the moment with the lawyers allocated to take witnesses because all the lawyers who are in this case are also taking witnesses in the Brdjanin case where we're still on the Prijedor aspect. And we allocated witnesses on the basis of the ones we were told would be called this week to certain lawyers. Because of the changes the lawyers who were going to do different ones are now on the Brdjanin case and so next week. I said that's a more minor problem, but it is one that we think could be avoided. So We would ask very much that in future after this period there aren't these sudden changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And in addition, we should recall that we would expect more detailed summaries of the expected testimony of the witnesses and that it is really based on earlier statements. I don't want to reopen the discussion of the last witness we heard before the recess. We had some problems with this. So we would appreciate if the summary really provides us with more detailed information. I think it was also a point raised by the Prosecution before the Court recess. If necessary, we should discuss this question either in closed session or within the framework of the 65 ter (i) meeting. Related to the three witnesses of this week, I think we can or better said, we have to live with that what we have before us. And in principle, we should be ready to start, and I see the Prosecution nodding. So therefore, there seems to be no impediment to start. Any other issues to be discussed by the Defence before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is one issue, Your Honour, if I may, that arose during the last session before the recess. During the -- if I may ask the question now. During the cross-examination of the last witness, the OTP, in our view, went beyond the parameters of the indictment and asked questions of certain allegations or bad conduct of Dr. Milomir Stakic which were not included in the indictment. The answer that was given truthful, and our position is consistent with the testimony of that. However, we believe that it taints and poisons the proceedings if the Prosecution is allowed to ask unsubstantiated and questions which can taint and cloud the issues before us, specifically during our case. The question arose upon an allegation of whether or not Dr. Stakic was involved in any humanitarian aid issues and involved with any criminal activity relating to that. That question in our view is inappropriate because there's no basis for that. There has been no allegation of that within the indictment. There has never been testimony from any of the OTP witnesses relating to that. Our concern is that the OTP will regrettably continue to ask questions far afield from the indictment and questions that the Court when we asked of witnesses and we were confined not to ask those questions without significant proof to be shown prior, we would ask that the same rules apply to the OTP and they be confined and restricted from asking such questions unless they can establish and are willing to amend their complaint to bring those allegations and charges which we believe are not truthful and should not be brought before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't here for that obviously, but can I say this: It's open to the Defence to object at any stage to any question that's asked in the course of cross-examination. The OTP can then make clear its basis for asking the question and Your Honour can rule. I think to try and make a generalised ruling like this as it were in theory is not very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply, this Court has consistently ruled generally to apply certain -- a certain form and manner in which we should proceed in this case. This Court has generally ruled that we should not ask questions that go beyond certain allegations within the fourth amended complaint, granted several of our oral and written motions in connection with that. We think it's prejudicial to the Defence to have the OTP ask such questions. The Defence does object to those questions, and we're objecting now for any future questions because we think it distracts from what this Court's duties are. It distracts from the job of the Defence. Certainly when the question was asked, it was taken by surprise. The Defence however knows what the answer would be by the witnesses from those questions, but it's certainly unnecessary and irrelevant to ask questions of both purported prior bad acts and subsequent bad acts or criminal conduct if they are not alleged in the indictment. These allegations have not been alleged. If the Court remembers specifically, when there was an exhibit that the OTP wanted to introduce which had some summaries from a certain commission where they discussed certain far-reaching allegations against individuals including Dr. Stakic, the Court rejected that report because it was not consistent and was not confined to the charges brought, the charges which we were discharged to defend upon. We did allow that question to proceed. The prejudice is not that that question was asked, because we heard the answer; the prejudice comes because the OTP in our view will continue to ask these questions and they should be prohibited from asking those questions consistent with the Court's general ruling as it related to the cross-examination by the Defence of the OTP witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the only appropriate way is indeed to intervene if you deem it necessary. Sometimes the Chamber intervenes ex officio in both directions, and we heard the reaction that this would destroy the flow of questioning the witness and the flow of question and answer. So I think we can only rule on the basis of question by question. Maybe some questions are related to the credibility. And therefore may be admissible. And finally, please take into account this is not a jury. Here are professional Judges, and we know that we can base our judgement only on relevant issues and relevant answers; and even though there might be a misleading question and an answer, not directly related to the fourth amended indictment, then immediately we will regard this as irrelevant and it will never appear in our summaries. And therefore, you can take it that there was no prejudice for Dr. Stakic. But we are aware that the Defence will, in principle, intervene more than Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they did in the past related to these questions mentioned before. Let me finally draw your attention that we all work on the same basis. Hopefully, you all have got the new amendments to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of 23 December, 2002, which entered into force the 1st of January, or better, the 30th of December already last year. There are a number of amendments, and we should know about the common basis of our work. You are in the possession of these amendments?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time we're not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I should say nor are we. But I had heard one of the rule changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to make it as easy as possible, I give one copy to Madam Registrar with the kind request that the usher please reproduces the necessary number of copies for the parties during the break. I think it's not appropriate to start the hearing of the first witness before the break. And therefore, we should have this break now, and the trial stays adjourned until 10.45.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope Your Honours will forgive if I leave at this stage but I have to deal with other matters, but Mr. Koumjian is dealing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you would be prepared to come back immediately in case we are discussing plea bargaining.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll be watching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start hearing the witness, after deliberations during the break, the Trial Chamber orders the hearing of Ms. Plavsic as soon as possible and as soon as practicable, we'll say immediately after the sentencing in her case as a witness in the case against Dr. Stakic. We will give a detailed order including the concrete day and hour of the hearing as soon as possible, but it should be quite clear that it would be either the same day of the sentencing or the following day in order to avoid that she has to be brought back to The Hague from another country. This means at the same time that the parties and the Trial Chamber have to be prepared for this hearing; and therefore, we kindly ask the Prosecution to disclose the statements in full to the Defence and the Trial Chamber, and as well, the entire plea agreement entered into by the OTP and Ms. Plavsic in the past. Second, as relates to the witnesses of next week, the Trial Chamber needs to re-emphasise that there is no additional discretion for days without witnesses. And whenever we can assist Defence counsel in bringing witnesses to The Hague, please let us know. But there will be no possibility at all to waste one or another day the next week or in the future. In case there should be no witness available, the Trial Chamber would take the opportunity to discuss legal issues emanating from the fourth amended indictment now in the light of not that what you have already seen under Rule 98 bis, but in the light of the view of the Judges having to decide finally on this case. And there are a number of legal questions. We deplore the fact that we are compelled to decide on sometimes even academic questions, but maybe the discussion of these legal questions will help us that the one or other question can be resolved immediately the one or other way. But please, take it that there will be hearings the entire next week. Having said that, we can start with the next witness. May I ask, are there any changes as regards protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. For this witness we don't have protective measures; only at one point in time, we'll ask to go to a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's, I start carefully, 54, Ms. Nadja Markovska?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the usher to escort Ms. Markovska into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Markovska. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we then please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. And as to the fact that you're a Defence witness, may I ask the Defence to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Markovska.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you just state for the record your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Nada Markovska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We speak the same language. For the benefit of the interpreters, I would like to ask you to please just wait for a bit before the translation is done. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: On the 3rd of March, 1950.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Donja Gradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Municipality?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the Omarska case?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A member of which party?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The Communists League of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the Communists League, were you ever a member of any other party?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you completed your education as typist, where did you first start working and when?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: That was in 1967, the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Dubica. In 1971, I started working for the Ministry of the Interior, Public Security Station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You retired at one point, and then you resumed work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: At the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've worked there since 1971 in fact continually filling the same position?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 1992, you also worked at the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which department was that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Crime police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of June 1992, was the place where you actually worked outside the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you then transferred to continue with your work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I was transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person to be transferred to Omarska, or were other colleagues of yours also transferred?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The whole of the service I worked for, I was transferred as the typist, and my inspectors were transferred, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other typists also transferred?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any order you to go to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Simo Drljaca's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: He was chief of the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start work in Omarska approximately? Or if you can remember a particular event that marked the beginning of your work there.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: One or two days following the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the investigation centre in Omarska already in operation at that time, that's even before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know. When I came, I came there to work with my colleagues from before. What it had been before the time we arrived and how it operated, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the incident when the inhabitants of Omarska tried to prevent the setting up of the investigation centre in their own village?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days prior to your arrival that had been, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I think that may have been five or six days prior to my arrival there, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us at what time your working day in Omarska began and when it ended?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Outside the public security station in Prijedor, we would be picked up by a bus at 8.00 and taken to the investigation centre in Omarska. We finished work around 5.00 in the afternoon, but that depended on what there was to be dealt with, some urgent issues, perhaps. In that case, we would stay longer, and then we would go to the restaurant where we would take a meal. That was lunch for us. And then we would be returned again outside the public security station in Prijedor, sometimes at 6.00, at 7.00, and sometimes even as late as 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days a week did you work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: There were no free days. We worked every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where inside Omarska was your office located precisely?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It was in the administrative building. You take a staircase up to the first floor. There was a toilet there, and next to the toilet, there was the office in which I worked as a typist together with a workmate of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you often leave that office?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you actually see from that office? What was your view through the window?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I could see the area outside the building with fountains. I don't know what I should call it exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any people who were imprisoned inside the investigation centre use these fountains, as you said?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you share your room with any of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have separate offices which were different from the ones where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did your work in Omarska entail?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I copied statements. Investigators would take statements from the inmates, and then we would type them and send the copies back to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally present at any of the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the investigators ever dictate the statements -- their notes to you directly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, not to me personally, but one of my colleagues did take their notes occasionally depending on the degree of urgency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from which different services or departments the inspectors present in Omarska came from?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us from which different services these inspectors were.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Public security, state security, and the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who headed the public security department? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the name of the gentleman who was at the head of the public security service?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Ranko Mica [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just repeat his name. The name in the record is not correct.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ranko Mijic also your boss?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there were inspectors from the state security sector there, too?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who their superior was, who they took their orders from?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Mirko Jesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mirko Jesic's superior?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: His superiors were in Banja Luka, but they coordinated matters with Simo Drljaca in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were also members of the military security there, weren't there? Who was at the head of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Mr. Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a military person himself, wasn't he, a military official?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the inspectors, were there any police officers in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did those policemen come from, from which units? From where did they come to the investigation centre? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: From the Omarska police station and from the reserve police forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the Omarska police department. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military present there?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any people there who had been employed in the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the working conditions for you there at that time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The situation was difficult. The room was small, and it was hot. The room was much frequented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with that, did you complain to anyone, and to whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: We complained to our bosses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your complaints after a while bear any fruit?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, there was nothing you could change about the situation. There was no electricity. We used an aggregate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please show the witness Exhibit Number S15-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be put on the ELMO immediately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, if usher would be so kind to move the picture a bit away from you, away, in the other direction. Thanks a lot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Markovska, this is only a model, so it doesn't reflect the reality. It may prove a bit difficult for you to get your bearings. Can you recognise any of the buildings in this image?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building to your right is the administrative building and the restaurant. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you use the image and point to the exact spot where your office was?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I think it was around here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the side where the restaurant was?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it's the other way around. This is where the restaurant was. If you can just turn this away for me, please. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We can take another picture, please. It's S15-18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you can see a bit clearer which is the smaller and which is the larger building. Can you now try to show us in this photograph where your office was.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I thought this was blown up. And then here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're pointing at is the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. And we used to go in this way here, we would pass through the restaurant. Yes. So that means that puts me about here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this photograph, the furthest section of the photograph from you in the upper right part of the building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your office looked out into the other side opposite the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain now how exactly you got into the building, where exactly you got into the building when the bus brought you there and where was the bus?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It would come this way, take this route, and this is where it usually pulled over. We got off the bus, and we used a door that's supposed to be here somewhere, the restaurant door. If it was open, we would go through the kitchen and enter the restaurant. But most of the times, the windows were open so we could just get in through the window, enter the restaurant, and then we would take the staircase to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just leave the photograph there for a moment, please. We can leave it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the usher's assistance will not be needed for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your office, could you actually see the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you see the section, the area known as pista?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the white house?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you took one of your meals inside the Omarska compound -- I mean inside the administrative building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us exactly where this room was where you took that meal.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It was the biggest room. I think hereabouts, yes, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the lower left corner, so to speak, of the administrative building on the first floor. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid-July or maybe in the second half of July, a delegation from Banja Luka arrived in the investigation centre Omarska. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the members of that delegation were? I mean, did you know or recognise anyone from that delegation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who you recognised.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior, Mr. Zupljanin; Mr. Simo Drljaca; and Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were accompanied by other people, too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the delegation came to Omarska, can you show us exactly where you were when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means in the room where you took your meal regularly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the room which is in the lower left corner of the administrative building in this photograph. Were there any persons who arrived with that particular group of people whom you knew particularly well?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: That was Minister Zupljanin's driver, a person I used to work with earlier. His name was Boro Nedimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the delegation reached the administrative building, they entered the administrative building, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your location when the delegation reached the first floor of the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: My colleague and I returned to our office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the delegation pass by your office?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the room where you used to take your meals, could you also see people leaving cars?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us exactly where the cars pulled over when the delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just indicated a spot which is on the opposite side from the so-called pista parallel to the shorter wall of the restaurant. Did you at any moment -- I apologise. I will reiterate my question. Did you ever prior to that day know Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first know about Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: After the election when he was appointed the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked very close to him from the moment when he was appointed the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir. My building and the building of the Municipal Assembly, yes, that is, my window faced the building of the Municipal Assembly. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you often see Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him well enough to be able to recognise him, and what was the best-known characteristic of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him, and he is bald, and that is what differentiates him from other men, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen him in Omarska? Would you have recognised him?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day when the delegation from Banja Luka arrived, did you amongst other people, either among the people leaving the cars or the people passing by your office, did you see Dr. Stakic there?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt, because also from your point of view the transcript may be misleading because you put two questions to the witness at the same time. So therefore, it reads: "Had you seen him in Omarska?" And "Would you have recognised him?" And the answer to both questions would be "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you have recognised Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him that day in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Your previous question, did you see him in Omarska? And now you added that day. Just for clarification, did you ever see Dr. Stakic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I should answer your question, sir, then. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long did the delegation stay in the administrative building in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the stay of that delegation, what was going on outside the building?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The inmates who were in the investigation centre, I could hear them singing. I couldn't see them, but I could hear them singing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now focus on the 30th of April, 1992, when the power was taken over in Prijedor by the SDS. After the taking over of power in Prijedor, did your colleagues in the Ministry of the Interior continue working with you?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: What colleagues do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everybody continue working regardless of their religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, everybody continued coming to work without any restrictions or -- everybody came to work regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After some time, did Muslims and Croats stop coming to work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they do of their own will, or were they dismissed? I am talking about the period from the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: They were not dismissed. They decided not to come to work of their own will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they asked to sign a paper on loyalty or a statement on loyalty?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we were all asked to sign such a paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to sign a similar paper when you first started working for the SUP and later on MUP?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, but some year or so later, I was asked to sign a paper like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Omarska, did you bring parcels to some of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your other colleagues do the same? Did they also bring parcels to the inmates in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that something that was happening on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody punished because of that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst working in Omarska, did you have a choice not to go to work there?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that actually your work obligation during the war?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your other colleagues also given war assignment or work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, did you ask for a temporary replacement?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you go to to ask for that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of the person who would replace you from time to time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Nevenka Sikman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst working in Omarska, did you talk to somebody in Prijedor about what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you bound by the rules not to talk to anybody about what was going on during the investigation procedure?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Omarska investigation centre, did you hear the moaning or wailing of people that would look like somebody being beaten up by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see people on the corridors being taken from the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they show the marks of injuries?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would just like to correct. I asked "some of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of them showed the marks of injuries?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which period of time of the existence of the investigation centre Omarska were there more of such incidents? And who were the people who were responsible for beating the inmates more than others?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: That was at the beginning. It was done by the inspectors whom I didn't know. I didn't know their names. I only heard their nicknames. They called each other by nicknames, and I didn't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But those were not your colleagues from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, was there a military unit from Banja Luka in the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the military police with their vehicles and weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who their commander was?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: They were under the command of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that group driven away from Omarska after a certain number of days?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how long they stayed there?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: 15 to 17 days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they responsible for the beating of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also responsible for the robbing of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I would like to go to private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a number of years, you have worked for the Ministry of the Interior. Do you know whether the person in the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly before the war, like, for example, Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, could such a person issue orders to the police, that is, to the employees of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic between April and September 1992 entering the MUP building at any time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Milomir Stakic ever give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Dr. Milomir Stakic ever issued any orders to anybody from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such event, but he was not in the position to issue any orders to anybody in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the end of the war, was the president of the Municipal Assembly in the position to issue any orders to any of the members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this did not change, the situation was the same before the war, during the war, and after the war?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first ten days or so, were people released from the investigation centre after they were questioned?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the period prior to the 30th of April, 1992. And let me ask you this: Are you aware of the fact that people from Prijedor and Prijedor municipality abandoned the area of Prijedor and left for Croatia and to the west?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that fact. It was happening on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they were picked up by buses who took them in that direction?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The collection point was in front of the Balkan Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Milomir Stakic either on television or on radio delivering a speech?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, as far as I can understand B/C/S, you indeed answered yes the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the takeover of power, did a dispatch come to the Prijedor MUP and was there a meeting in connection with such a dispatch in the Prijedor MUP?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who brought that dispatch to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that person or persons?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question? Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that person, the person who brought the dispatch or who received the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: His name was Milos Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the dispatch read out at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to remember, but maybe you do remember who the dispatch was from?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The dispatch was from the Minister of the Interior from Sarajevo, and his name was Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the dispatch was read?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The employees were outraged by the content of that dispatch, and they left the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In rough outlines, do you remember the content of the dispatch, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I remember roughly that it was an order to set up checkpoints to prevent the military from passing through or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive any order or request from the Crisis Staff of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever send any reports to the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of anyone from the Ministry of the Interior in Prijedor submitting sporadically or continually reports to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Vahid Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: He worked in the warehouse where the weapons and equipment of the Public Security Station Prijedor were kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was going on in 1991 and 1992? What was the reason why you mentioned this gentleman's name to me?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: In addition to active-duty, regular police officers, we also had reserve forces, police stations. And in early 1992, the members of those forces would be summoned to the station, and they were given weapons. When Mr. Talundzic became chief, I think the number of reserve police forces increased, both Muslims and others. And then for a while, you could see large groups of such people coming there to get their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By and large, what ethnicity were the members of the reserve police forces?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: All ethnic groups were represented. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who did you notice was given the most weapons, which group?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: To Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Markovska. This concludes our direct examination, our examination-in-chief. Now you will be examined by our colleagues from the Prosecution, and also the Honourable Judges may have a question or two at the end of your testimony. So please, remain seated. Yes, say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just leave to use the facilities, please? Is that allowed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we want to take a break now. And the trial stays adjourned until 12.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Just for the record, we forgot before entering the courtroom the last time that we have to add to the transcript that Ms. Sutherland is also representing now the Prosecution once again. Welcome, and also a good New Year on behalf of the Chamber for you, Ms. Sutherland. Then may I give the floor for the cross-examination when the witness is in the courtroom to the OTP. But at the same time, tell you that we decided not, ex officio, or propo moto as it reads, to issue a warning under Rule 91, but whenever the Prosecution feels that it would be necessary, please do so. We don't want to interrupt your cross-examination. May the usher please bring in the witness once again. Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Markovska.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Markovska, where were you on the 30th of April, 1992, the day of the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I was at home in my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning, as usual, I did go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to us exactly what your position was prior to that day? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I worked as a typist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the SJB building in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It was the crime police department where I worked, and Ranko Mijic was my boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
