utterances.text: On that day, can you describe what you saw when you arrived at work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: In the centre on my way to work, I saw a number of police officers. That's around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the building where you worked, did things appear as they normally did in the centre of town in front of the SJB building in front of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I think there were flags there, flags had been put up. I think so, at least. And there were more police officers there as usual, as compared to any other ordinary day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those police officers of mixed ethnicity typical of how the police department had been prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I didn't really pay attention. I didn't look. I was just on my way to work. That's until I reached the building. I didn't really think it very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you got to the building and worked that day, did you notice whether the people that you were working with were the same people that you had been working with the day before, that all the police officers maintained their positions?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, they all came to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslim police officers disarmed that day?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I just went straight to where I worked. What happened to them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't notice any changes within the police department following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Hasan Talundzic. He was the chief of police of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't a professional policeman. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, he was the chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, what I meant by my question was he hadn't been a police officer prior to being named the chief. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your understanding that he was proposed by the SDA party to be the chief of police of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't someone well-known in Bosnia, but he was proposed by the local SDA to take over the position of chief of police in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that everyone continued to come to work regularly, I presume do you mean that the chief of police, Mr. Talundzic, the boss, continued to come to work regularly and maintained his position after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I don't know about that particular day, but I think the next day he did not show up. The next day, Mr. Drljaca came. But I really can't remember whether he came to work on that particular day or not because I did not work with him directly. I worked in my own section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what professional contacts you had, and professional relationship you had, with Mr. Drljaca. And I'm not limiting myself to before the takeover; I mean throughout his career in Prijedor, what contacts did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Official contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at least let us start with official contacts, yes.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first contact was when I worked in Omarska, when I asked to be replaced. We didn't have the weekends off, we had no time to rest. So of course, if anything needed typing, he would write it up and give it to me to type it. That's the sort of contact we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct that you were more or less the personal secretary of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, you couldn't say that. He had a secretary. I was only the typist. But as I had been in service for a long time as a professional, and I was one of the best typists around, whenever there was something to be typed up quickly, and a good quality work to be done in terms of typing, those things would usually be given to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Drljaca prior to him becoming the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no, that's when I first met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Drljaca, like Mr. Talundzic, had not been a professional policeman before taking that position; he was a lawyer who worked for the schools. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that put Mr. Drljaca in that position?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I think the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took power on the 30th of April, 1992? Who was in control of Prijedor following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the SDS chose Mr. Drljaca, you mean the local party? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who became the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person who was the highest civilian authority in the municipality after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were not Mr. Drljaca's secretary. So would it be correct that you don't know, you were not present when he was given instructions and you were not present at his meetings? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Crisis Staff. Do you know if Mr. Drljaca was on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I referred to the Crisis Staff in the context of Omarska because there you had the public security, the state security, and the military security. I don't know about the existence of any other staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, and don't you know, that Mr. Stakic headed the Crisis Staff that took over power in Prijedor following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct and don't you know that Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Arsic from the military were members of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think that could be because as a typist, you were not informed of who was giving -- who was giving orders and controlling things in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, they didn't really keep me informed. And that wasn't part of my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still work with the police in Prijedor. Can you tell us regarding Mr. Drljaca when he stopped being the chief of police and when he came back again as the chief of police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact time, but I know that he was in that position for a while and then he was replaced, and then he was back again but I can't give you the exact time frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct that he left at the same time that Dr. Stakic stepped down as the president of the municipality, and he came back when Dr. Stakic came back as the president of the municipality at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that information at all. First time I hear of it, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In 1997, Mr. Drljaca was the chief of police in Prijedor. Correct? In 1996, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't claim anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about working at Omarska for three months. Can you tell us if you saw any persons you recognised among the prisoners in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I believe about -- at least 50 per cent of them knew me, but I explained to you the way we would go in. So I tried -- well, it wasn't very pleasant meeting those people over there. There was nothing you could do to help them but you had to be there and do what you were supposed to be doing. I did recognise a number of faces, and there were persons I failed to recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also as part of your responsibilities, you had to type reports regarding interrogations of these prisoners, and you had to type lists of these prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The work that you did at Omarska was organised. You were given transportation from the centre of town to Omarska. You kept regular hours. And you were paid by the police, according to your work. And you reported according to a chain of command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: They didn't really pay us. I think for two years, we -- none of us were paid. My responsibility was to go to work, do my job, and answer to my boss. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that at Omarska, you saw that there was a coordination of military police from Banja Luka, the state security department, and the crime suppression department. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, both the state security department and crime suppression department in Prijedor both came under the command of the chief of police Simo Drljaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Their task was to go -- well, actually, I think there was an investigator from the public security, my own service, in one room; and in the other, there was an investigator from the state security. And that was how they worked. So probably Jesic was the person they talked to in order to coordinate and organise matters, but I really can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the names of the prisoners that you saw, among the prisoners that you saw or the names that you saw on the reports or lists that you typed, did you recognise the names of prominent persons from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: How should I explain this? During the years I spent working, I've typed up a whole lot of things. And the next day I would never remember all the things I typed the day before. There isn't a chance in hell really of me remembering. I was just trying to do my work as conscientiously as possible. I couldn't really remember such things. There wasn't really -- sorry. What I was about to say was that I didn't really go to the centre of town very much. I was more of a family person. I just went to work. And the nature of my work was such that they could call me even after working hours and during holidays to go back to my work and do something. So I didn't have many opportunities to socialise. But many people knew me as the person who worked in that particular position. So I knew some of the faces, but sometimes I didn't know the names. And I wasn't really in touch with any of the public figures or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you knew who Muhamed Cehajic was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the president of the municipality of Prijedor prior to the takeover, Mr. Cehajic, in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I didn't see him, but I believe he was there, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know he was there because that was common knowledge in the camp, isn't it, that the president of the municipality was a prisoner in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, it's impossible for me to tell you now. I really can't remember, but I suppose that yes, he was there. I didn't personally see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that Becir Medunjanin and his wife were in the camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any doctors that you knew in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I saw Dr. Ivic, and there was another technician. I can't remember his name. And there was yet another doctor, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Sadikovic, Eso Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, did you see dead bodies in and around the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any dead bodies, not during the time that we were there. I explained to you exactly how we went into the building, and on my way back home from work, I just didn't notice anything. So maybe, if there was anything, it occurred after we had already left work. Personally, I really didn't see anything, honestly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you aware that people were being killed in the Omarska camp during those precise months that you were working at the camp, June, July, and August?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I heard stories later that such things had indeed taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the summertime. Did you smell bodies decomposing when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no. The only smell I could feel was the chloride that the cleaning ladies used to clean the premises to keep infections from spreading because it was very hot and you could feel the stench of sweat. So that's what you could notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a person who typed up things for Mr. Drljaca, did you become familiar with his signature? Did he sign these letters and documents?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Once I believe I did type something up for him, but whether he signed it later or not, I really don't know. For example, since I worked in the department where I worked, if it was a criminal report I was supposed to type up, then usually there would be the title "Chief of the Public Security Station" so he may have signed something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me if I misunderstood you, but I thought when you were discussing your relationship with Mr. Drljaca, you said that he would bring you things to type for him.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, once I think, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now a document marked S107.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please show the witness 107B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being prepared, ma'am, if I could just ask you, who do you think had better knowledge of who set up the Omarska camp, you or Mr. Drljaca? Who would have been in a better position to know?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, certainly Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you could please take a look at this document, S107, take your time, and you may read all of it, but I would ask you in particular to look at the introduction and first paragraph, and then --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not going to read this. No. I mean, I know how I type, and I don't use this method. I leave a wide margin at the end, so there's no need for me to go through this. I can tell you right now for certain that I was not the one who typed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't asked you that question, at least not yet. Please look at the document, read the introduction and the first paragraph. And ma'am, if you could look at the last page also.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I understand from your earlier remark that you did not type this document. Do you recognise this, though, as a copy of a document from the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: This is Simo's signature. Now, who typed this up, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if the ELMO could be -- never mind. Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ma'am, then if you -- having read the first paragraph where this document indicates that "the Omarska strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operational information, together with the introduction which indicates that with a view to the speedy and effective establishment of peace on the territory of Prijedor municipality, and in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, I hereby order the following," would you now change your opinion as to who it was that ordered the establishment of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no, I would not change my opinion. Simo Drljaca was the chief of the Prijedor Public Security Station, and the public security station had a security station -- a public security headquarters in Banja Luka. And then their superiors were in the Ministry of the Interior in Banja Luka. I think that was the hierarchy. So even if this was done, it couldn't have been done without their orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your opinion that when Mr. Drljaca wrote that this was done in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, that he was wrong, that he was lying? What is your opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't think anything. I just gave you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's based upon your professional experience as a typist for the police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you -- when you went to the Omarska camp to work every day, did you travel on a paved road to get to the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: There were two roads. I am not a driver, so I can't tell you exactly. But there were occasions when we would take the so-called scenic route through some villages, and there were times when we would go from Prijedor towards Banja Luka and on that way we would reach Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you never saw anyone, any dead bodies, any corpses, at the camp. Did you ever hear any shots at the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the context, what happened when you heard gunshots?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I would hear a noise, and that would happen during the time when the military police from Banja Luka were there. That's what I already told you. They were armed. I don't understand weapons, so I can't tell you exactly what they had. But they had tanks and other tools and vehicles, and they surrounded the entire building, and we were scared. And sometimes, they would fire. They would create a lot of disrest, and they would instill nervousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would people inside the building simply ignore the shooting, just go on with their work?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I was in my office, and what others did, I really don't know, Whether somebody else intervened or not. I only know that people from the public and state security complained to the representative of the military, and they asked them to do something so as to stop these things because people were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But in your office, people -- the office you were in, people ignored the shooting?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: How could you ignore that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never had the impression that the shooting was directed at you or people in the building; correct? This was something you thought was going on among the police and the prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: At one point, it was directed at us. But that's the kind of military they were. I don't know who they were. I only suppose that they came from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever evacuated from the building? You said you worked every day, so I presume that they never took you away from the building. You came to work every day there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know why they would evacuate us. I don't know what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never felt that the mine was being -- the camp was being attacked by an outside group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't think too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came in by bus every day and went out every day, they didn't tell you to duck, look for cover, be careful of snipers; you just would walk to the bus, get on the bus, and go home or come in, get off the bus, and go to work. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I've already told you that we would take two roads. When the situation was still dangerous, for 15 or 20 days, we would take a detour through villages. I suppose this was for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What days were those? You said for 15 days or so. Was that in June when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the visit of the foreign journalists to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when they visited? What do you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I didn't leave my office at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your perspective, was it a typical day?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: A typical day, just like any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was escorting the journalists?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I only heard that they came. I didn't leave my office. I was very busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that true pretty much of every day, you had a lot of work to do? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. Slavica Lakija [phoen] and I worked together, and I spent more time in that office whereas she would leave more often. She had more time, and I had to work. That's the kind of a person I am. I'm diligent, responsible. And when I am given a task to do, I do it quickly. If I am given something to type I do it. And I was given a lot of work to do. There was no electricity. There was no gas. Things would go wrong. And tasks had to be performed, so I thought I should perform them as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about the visit in July of Mr. Brdjanin to the camp, and Mr. Zupljanin. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin was the president of the regional Crisis Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Brdjanin was an important politician from Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I only knew my minister, and I recognised him. Him and Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told us that Mr. Brdjanin was in this delegation. Did you recognise Mr. Brdjanin from television?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, later on, I saw him on TV. I hadn't seen him on TV by then. But later on. At that time, I didn't watch television. I didn't listen to the radio. There was no electricity, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you didn't -- how long did you look at the delegation? You were looking from the first floor window. And can you tell us how long you saw them?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: While they were standing there, we saw a colleague of ours, the driver. Then we went back to our office. We knew that they would be passing by our office, so we came back into our office. The door was open. Then they passed by, and the colleague, the driver, entered our office. And he was a bit embarrassed to see the inmates and to hear them sing. Our window was open, and you couldn't see them easily. You had to lean over to see them. The driver had a few boxes of cigarettes on him, and he threw them out of the window. That's a detail that still lingers in my mind, and he stayed in our office for a brief period of time after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw the delegation, or at least part of it, walking down the hallway. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also saw them for a brief period of time from your window, would that be correct, getting out of the cars?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many cars and how many people do you think arrived in that delegation in total?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't tell you actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's because it wasn't a detail at the time that was particularly important to you, and it has been ten years since then. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It wasn't important. I think that there wasn't just one car or two cars. There must have been three or maybe more. But I can't tell you exactly how many there were. But I'm sure that there wasn't just one car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is possible that there were people in that delegation that you didn't see. Isn't that correct, didn't notice?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: All who were in the delegation, they came out of the cars, and they climbed the stairs, and they came upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you were first asked whether Mr. Stakic was a member of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: What do you mean "when"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I understand from your testimony today that it's your -- at the present time, you're saying that you don't remember seeing Mr. Stakic in that delegation. When was it that you first were asked to remember who was in the delegation? Was it -- please allow me to finish. Was it last month, was it last year when someone first asked you "Was Mr. Stakic in the delegation"?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was that somebody asked me for the first time about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why you would remember Mr. Stakic being in the delegation? Would you expect him as the president of the municipality to have been there and you were surprised not to see him? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, no. Actually, I didn't know him before the war. I've already told you. When he became the vice-president, then I learned that his name was Dr. Stakic. I didn't have any contacts with him. Now you're asking me how I know that he went there. What I can say to that is that he is somebody that I would remember had he been there. But I'm sure that he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it that you would remember Dr. Stakic if he had been in that delegation that visited the camp during one day of the three months that you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Because that was a specific delegation with Mr. Minister as a member of that delegation. So that was a very important delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Minister," you mean Mr. Zupljanin who was the head of the CSB in Banja Luka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Zupljanin, and you said you didn't know him at the time but you later learned of Mr. Brdjanin, that you would expect important persons from Banja Luka like that that when they visited, it was a matter of importance in Prijedor to have a visit from someone like Mr. Zupljanin? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that they came to see -- and I've already told you when I first went there, we were told that we would stay there only for a short period of time, the time went on. And I suppose that the delegation came to inspect the conditions of work. I don't know what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, would you expect someone from the Prijedor government to meet and greet Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Brdjanin when they came to Prijedor because of their importance?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, Simo Drljaca was there, the chief of the police. And I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown another document, and that is S353.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, just take your time, please. I'd like you to just look that over, and I'm going to ask you two questions when you've had a chance to review it. First, whether you recall seeing this before or typing it, and second, whether it appears to be a document from the Prijedor police, according to the formatting that you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I didn't type this. The heading is "The Public Security Station in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the last page, do you recognise the signature of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not something that I typed, and I am a hundred per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And if the witness could then be shown S130.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we leave that document, I may have a few questions for her. Madam, do you recall the attack -- do you recall the 22nd of May there being an incident at Hambarine, and the next day an attack on the village of Hambarine taking place?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear in the media, on the radio or in the newspaper, any demands of the villages of Hambarine prior to the attack? In other words, did someone order them to surrender weapons or surrender individuals?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I believe that an order had been issued for them to surrender something to the checkpoints. They were asked to surrender the perpetrators of some crimes that had been committed, and I believe that the crimes involved some dead and injured people. So the army asked them to surrender the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually hear the announcement on the radio demanding the surrender?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't have a radio. I just heard it from other fellow employees, because it was in the vicinity. We could hear shots. And I heard from my colleagues what had happened and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said it was a crime that was committed. Is it correct that the police were also involved in investigating what happened? Were they involved at all in the incidents in Hambarine to your knowledge? I'm not asking you to guess. If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I really can't remember, and it wouldn't be fair for me to guess or speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look at page 2 of that document that you have in front of you, it's the page marked on the right with the number, top right B0032579, and you look at the last paragraph beginning with "Obzirom". It indicates, isn't that correct, that it indicates that "since the citizens of the village of Hambarine did not respect the decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic, did not surrender their arms, refused to cooperate with the legal organs of government over the attack on the soldiers, and rejected demands the army made to them, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor decided on military intervention in this village, to disarm and capture the known perpetrators of the crimes against the soldiers."

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar as an employee of the police station headed by Mr. Drljaca who wrote this report that the Crisis Staff had ordered the attack on Hambarine? Or had asked the military to attack Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I was not familiar with all this. I don't know who had issued that order. This is not within my scope of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that precise answer. If you could now look at Exhibit S130 -- excuse me, I gave you the wrong number. S114. Sorry. While that's being done, ma'am, were you aware of anyone trying to get prisoners released from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I really wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of an order that no one could be released without the permission of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had testified that Mr. Drljaca did not report to the civilian authorities. Can you please take a look at this document S114 and, first, again please tell us, does this appear to be a document from the police of Prijedor signed by Mr. Drljaca, and second if you've seen it or typed this document yourself, if you've seen it previously or typed the document yourself?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't type it myself. I see this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct that you were not aware, if you look at this document now, that Mr. Drljaca wrote a report to the Crisis Staff reporting on the implementation of decisions of the Crisis Staff by the police?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your impression working at the Omarska camp that the names of each of the prisoners were recorded in documents?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: This is not what I was concerned with. I typed what I was told to type. There were some lists of inmates, but whether those were full lists containing all of their names, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you the lists that you had to type?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: In that building where we worked, there was Mijic, there was Jesic, and one of them would put together a list and bring it to us to type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the lists that you saw? I understand there were various lists, but would they be lists of ten names? Did it sometimes be more than a hundred names? Was it as much as several thousand names?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but obviously some lists were short, some were longer and were typed on several pages. But there were lists, and that's what I can remember, that we did type these lists of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a filing system? Were the documents kept at the camp? Were they sent to the public security station in Omarska or Prijedor? Were copies made? What do you recall about how the records were kept?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: All those things remained in the office where they worked. I didn't have to write any reports to anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about arriving at the camp about a day after the attack on Prijedor approximately, one or two days I believe you said, after the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attack on Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you had heard that the people who lived around the mine or in Omarska had objected to setting up the camp there five or six days before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. And there was even an attack on the police station in Omarska. There were even some people injured in that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this objection to setting up the camp happened several days before the attack on Prijedor by the Muslim and Croat force. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No. Actually, I don't know. This happened -- on the 22nd, there was this incident in Hambarine. On the 24th, it was in Kozarac. And after these events in Kozarac, I suppose that the first prisoners were supposed to be placed somewhere. And that all those things happened around that time, and that it was already at that time that somebody had decided that the place would be Omarska and that at the time, the villagers objected to that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think you've answered my question. Can you tell us, how many people were working in Omarska during the daytime when you were there? Can you give us an estimate? How many guards, how many personnel were at the camp including the secretaries, the typists, like yourself?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: It is rather difficult for me to say that. I remember that there were two of us who worked together. There were seven to eight officers for investigators, and each of them served as an office to two people. Then there were people in the headquarters. There were the police who provided security. I can't really tell you precisely how many people there were. It would be a pure guesswork if I attempted to give you an exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need an exact number, but would it be correct that there were dozens of people working, that there was military, police, that there were persons like yourself, typists?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think -- yes, what you say is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you never talked to people in Prijedor about what was going on in the investigation procedure, that you were told not to talk. Who told you not to talk to the people in Prijedor about what was going on in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: Nobody told me anything. I just simply worked for that service, and I knew what the service was all about. And secondly, there was nobody to talk to. I would leave my apartment early in the morning, I would come back late in the evening. There was no electricity. There was no water. I would just spend the night there, then I would go back to work the following morning, and there was nobody to talk to actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it a matter of common knowledge that you felt you didn't need to tell people that there were two or three thousand people, citizens of Prijedor, who were being held in a camp at the mine?

utterances.speaker: NADA MARKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't tell that to anybody because working for that service implied you didn't talk about things. That was considered normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I'm almost done. But if we take the break, I may have just one or two questions tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think there will be a number of questions remaining tomorrow. Therefore, I have to ask you to be so kind and to come once again tomorrow. Tomorrow, as you may know, we start not as scheduled at 9.00, but 9.30, that we can sit until 4.30 in the afternoon. Any other issues to be raised in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to warn the witness that she can not share with anybody what she told us today, that she is still under oath. There is another lady. She can not speak with her about the case. And I have to tell her, because she doesn't know, but we cannot contact her as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind not to contact any representative of the parties, not the Judges, not any other persons you by chance meet here in The Hague, and please don't discuss issues related to this case with anybody until tomorrow. Thank you for your understanding. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of January, 2003, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
